correctness.rationale: For all integers \(2\le a\le b\) the clique-size process has internal probability (x-1)/(2b-2a+3x+4k-1). Every internal choice skips a clique-size state and adds exactly one deficit unit. The all-cross probability is an exact telescoping-in-state product; vertex-label symmetry makes the conditional maximum matching uniform, giving whole-output total variation by disjoint supports. For \(b\ge4a\) an independent uniform sequence couples the visited internal choices to Bernoulli probabilities (x-1)/(2b); visits, skips and Le Cam inequality yield the explicit \(a(a-1)(14a-5)/(24b^2)\) bound. Logarithmic product estimates establish the sharp quadratic transition. Exact labeled enumeration, rational recursions, inequalities and numerical total variation pass VERIFY_OK 11717 assertions; finite tests corroborate but the general theorem follows from the displayed proof.

originality.rationale: The assessed claim is not the classical greedy algorithm or the classical Poisson approximation theorem. It is the fixed complete split-graph exact product, the conditional uniform injection law, whole-output total variation identity, and explicit quadratic Poisson-deficit transition. The two closely related full papers inspected address random bipartite inputs and sparse random graph/tree inputs, neither of which logically implies the split-graph statement. Searches revealed no matching exact law, although historical priority is not certified and the complete 1991 predecessor was inaccessible.
residual_risks: Uninspected portions of the 1991 Randomized Greedy Matching paper may contain stronger formulas or reductions.
The full historical literature on exact greedy matchings of dense split graphs is not exhaustively available.
The error bound is not asserted to have best constants.

value.rationale: Uniform-edge greedy maximal matching has a natural additive-optimality risk in a complete split graph: choosing a clique-internal edge destroys one potential cross match. The exact probability of losing zero matches, the full-law approximation by uniform optimum injections, and Poisson fluctuations at b on the order of \(a^2\) quantify algorithmic reliability in a high-imbalance regime. The \(b/a^2\) threshold and \(b\ge4a\) error bound supply natural phase information for an infinite two-population graph family; this is not merely a generic approximation theorem or one finite-table entry.
